Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

DENVER, Colorado (CNN)  -- Early indications show no problems with the landing gear, tires or brakes on the Continental Airlines jet that veered off a runway at Denver International Airport in Colorado, despite earlier reports. The wreckage of the Continental Airlines plane sits in a ravine December 22 in Denver, Colorado. "There's no indication from the physical examination on the scene of brake problems at this time," said Robert Sumwalt, a National Transportation Safety Board  member leading the investigation team. Saturday's accident injured more than three dozen people, including the captain who piloted the plane. Sumwalt said preliminary evidence indicated no problems with the Boeing 737's landing gear, tires or engines before the jet ran off the runway into a 40-foot-deep ravine during its take-off roll. Earlier Monday, a source with knowledge of the investigation told CNN that early indications suggested that a problem with the landing gear, tire or brakes may have caused the accident. The source said the problem could have caused a wheel to lock up or some other situation that would have made the plane veer off as it headed down the runway.  Watch what NTSB official has to say about flight recorders » . "The brakes showed no leaks, no locked brakes," Sumwalt told reporters late Monday, adding that the brake pads "looked good." He said tire marks indicate that all four main landing gear were inflated. The weather was clear, and no obstacles were on the runway, he said. The accident injured 38 people, most from bruises and broken bones as frightened passengers tried to flee a fire that broke out on board Flight 1404. No fatalities were reported. Sumwalt said the captain, an 11-year veteran of Continental, was injured in the accident and "not physically able" to be interviewed yet. But an investigator interviewed the first officer, who told them that the initial take-off roll and taxi was normal. The the co-pilot "noticed a deviation from the center line of the runway and a sudden left turn," Sumwalt said. An off-duty crew that flew the aircraft into Denver before the Saturday flight to Houston was also on board. The first officer from that crew said there was "absolutely no problem with the aircraft" during the previous flight. Sumwalt said the cockpit voice recorder "shows nothing out of the ordinary" during the preflight operations. He said the recording revealed that 41 seconds after the brakes were released, there were sounds of bumping and rattling. Four seconds later, a crew member called for a rejected takeoff. Flight 1404 was taking off about 6:18 p.m. Sumwalt said the plane reached a maximum speed of 119 knots (137 mph) before going into the ravine. Passengers on Sunday described the chaos inside the plane after the plane came to rest.  Watch survivor describe crash on blog » . "Some people were trying to get luggage from the top, the engine was on fire so I was worried, you know, about getting out of there," said Gabriel Trejos. "And then we had another guy yelling, 'Oh the plane's gonna blow up! The plane's gonna explode!' " Another passenger, Jeb Tilly, described the experience as "incredibly violent."  Watch first responders on the scene » . Trejos, who was traveling with his wife and baby, told CNN he sensed something was wrong with the plane before it took off. "I heard something over the intercom before, you know, that they were having engine problems and shortly after that they said that everything's fine ... there's going to be an on-time flight." Continental spokeswoman Julie King, however, told CNN that she was unaware of any announcement of engine problems on board the flight. Sumwalt agreed, saying, "I don't have any information, no one has come to us that they knew of a problem" before the accident.

**DENVER, Colorado (CNN)** — Contrary to earlier reports, an initial inspection found no evidence that problems with the landing gear, tires or brakes caused a Continental Airlines jet to leave a runway at Denver International Airport.

The remains of the Continental aircraft were visible in a ravine in Denver on December 22.

“At this point, the physical inspection at the scene has revealed no sign of brake trouble,” said Robert Sumwalt, the National Transportation Safety Board member heading the investigative team.

More than three dozen people were hurt in Saturday’s crash, including the captain flying the aircraft. According to Sumwalt, preliminary findings showed no apparent defects in the Boeing 737’s landing gear, tires or engines before it departed the runway during its takeoff run and plunged into a ravine 40 feet deep.

Earlier Monday, someone familiar with the inquiry told CNN that investigators initially believed a landing-gear, tire or brake malfunction might have contributed to the accident. That person said such a failure could have locked a wheel or created another condition that forced the aircraft to swerve while accelerating along the runway.

Speaking to reporters late Monday, Sumwalt said investigators found neither brake-fluid leaks nor locked brakes, and the brake pads appeared to be in good condition. Tire tracks also suggested that all four tires on the main landing gear were inflated. He added that skies were clear and the runway was free of obstructions.

The accident injured 38 people, mostly through bruises and broken bones, as terrified passengers attempted to escape a fire aboard Flight 1404. No one was killed.

Sumwalt said the captain, who had worked for Continental for 11 years, was injured and was not yet physically capable of being questioned. Investigators did interview the first officer, who reported that the taxi and the beginning of the takeoff run appeared normal.

The co-pilot then saw the aircraft drift away from the runway’s center line before abruptly turning left, Sumwalt said.

Also aboard was an off-duty crew that had flown the same plane into Denver before its scheduled Saturday trip to Houston. The first officer from that crew said the aircraft had experienced “absolutely no problem” during the earlier flight.

According to Sumwalt, the cockpit voice recorder captured nothing unusual during preflight procedures. The recording showed that bumping and rattling noises began 41 seconds after the brakes were released. Four seconds after those sounds started, a crew member ordered that the takeoff be aborted.

Flight 1404 began its takeoff at approximately 6:18 p.m. The jet reached a top speed of 119 knots, or 137 mph, before entering the ravine, Sumwalt said.

On Sunday, passengers recalled the disorder inside the aircraft once it stopped.

Gabriel Trejos said some travelers tried to retrieve bags from overhead compartments while an engine was burning, making him anxious to leave quickly. He also recalled another man shouting that the aircraft was going to explode.

A second passenger, Jeb Tilly, characterized the crash as “incredibly violent.”

Trejos, who was traveling with his wife and infant, told CNN that he had suspected something was wrong before departure. He said he heard an announcement over the intercom referring to engine trouble, followed soon afterward by another statement saying that everything was fine and the flight would leave on schedule.

Continental spokeswoman Julie King told CNN, however, that she knew of no announcement about engine problems aboard the flight. Sumwalt likewise said investigators had received no information from anyone indicating that a problem was known before the crash.

Investigators examining the crash of Continental Airlines Flight 1404 focused on physical evidence from the aircraft and runway, weather data, and statements from the flight crew. The Boeing 737 veered off Runway 34R while accelerating for takeoff at Denver International Airport, crossed rough terrain, and came to rest in a ravine, where it caught fire.

The flight, bound for Houston, was carrying passengers and crew when the accident occurred. Everyone escaped, although 38 people were injured and several required hospitalization. Despite the extensive damage to the aircraft, no one was killed.

Investigators documented tire marks and other evidence along the runway and the airplane’s path after it left the pavement. They inspected the landing gear, wheels, tires, brakes, steering system, flight controls, and engines for signs of a mechanical failure that could have caused the sudden loss of directional control. Preliminary findings showed that the tires were inflated before departure and that the brakes, landing gear, and engines appeared to have been operating normally.

Those findings contradicted early speculation that a blown tire, locked brake, landing-gear malfunction, or engine problem had forced the aircraft off the runway. Investigators also reviewed cockpit accounts and weather observations, paying particular attention to the strong, shifting winds reported around the airport at the time.

Although the initial examination ruled out several suspected mechanical causes, it did not immediately explain why the jet departed the runway. The investigation therefore continued, with officials analyzing wind conditions, crew actions, air-traffic-control information, and data recovered from the aircraft’s flight recorders.

## Continental 737 veers off Denver runway, burns; investigators cite powerful crosswind gust

**DENVER —** A Continental Airlines Boeing 737 carrying 115 people veered off a runway during takeoff from Denver International Airport, broke apart and caught fire, forcing passengers and crew to flee the burning aircraft in darkness and near-freezing weather.

The Houston-bound jet, operating as **Continental Flight 1404**, was accelerating on **Runway 34R on Dec. 20, 2008**, when it abruptly departed the left side of the pavement. The aircraft crossed uneven ground, struck airport equipment and came to rest in several sections roughly 2,000 feet from the runway.

All **110 passengers and five crew members survived**. Dozens were taken to hospitals, with injuries ranging from cuts and fractures to serious trauma. The captain was among those seriously injured.

> **Editor’s note:** The initial accident was reported as breaking news in 2008. The cause described below reflects the National Transportation Safety Board’s subsequent investigation and final findings.

### Takeoff turns into emergency

The Boeing **737-500**, registration **N18611**, had been cleared for takeoff when it began moving sharply left as its speed increased. Tire marks and wreckage evidence showed the aircraft left the runway before reaching flying speed.

After crossing rough terrain, the landing gear collapsed and the fuselage was extensively damaged. A post-crash fire consumed much of the right side of the aircraft, but passengers and crew were able to evacuate before flames spread through the cabin.

Airport firefighters arrived within minutes and extinguished the blaze. The rapid evacuation was credited with preventing fatalities despite the severity of the breakup and fire.

### Survivors describe violent motion and flames

Passengers later told reporters and investigators that the takeoff initially appeared routine before the aircraft began shaking and moving violently. Survivors described a sudden series of impacts, darkness inside the cabin, smoke and the sight of flames outside.

Some said overhead bins opened and luggage fell as the aircraft traveled across the rough ground. After it stopped, flight attendants shouted evacuation commands while passengers moved toward usable exits and climbed or slid onto the snow-covered field.

Several survivors recalled helping injured or disoriented passengers away from the burning wreckage. Others described standing in the cold while emergency crews searched the aircraft and transported the injured.

The NTSB’s survival investigation found that the fuselage damage created additional openings through which some occupants escaped. Investigators also noted that the fire developed after the aircraft left the runway, giving those aboard a crucial window to evacuate.

### Early focus on weather and directional control

Initial attention centered on Denver’s strong, shifting winds. Winds reported to the flight crew before departure were significant but remained within the limits then used by Continental for the 737.

Investigators later determined that the aircraft encountered a much stronger gust during its takeoff roll than the crew had been told to expect. Data and wind modeling indicated that the crosswind component rose sharply—possibly to about **36 knots**—as the aircraft accelerated.

The wind was associated with mountain-wave conditions east of the Rocky Mountains, which can produce rapid and localized changes in velocity. The strongest gust was not captured in the routine wind information passed to the pilots before takeoff.

No evidence emerged of an engine failure, tire failure or major mechanical defect that would independently explain the runway departure.

### NTSB: Captain stopped necessary rudder input

In its final report, the NTSB concluded that the probable cause was the captain’s **cessation of rudder input needed to maintain directional control** after the airplane was struck by the strong crosswind gust.

As the jet began turning left, the captain initially applied right rudder. But investigators found that the corrective input was not maintained or increased as required. With the aircraft traveling at high speed and still on the ground, the leftward deviation became unrecoverable before the crew could reject the takeoff effectively.

The safety board emphasized that the captain’s action did not occur in isolation. It identified several contributing factors:

- The unusually strong and rapidly changing crosswind gust.
- The air traffic control system’s use of wind information that did not adequately reflect the immediate conditions on the runway.
- Inadequate airline training and guidance for pilots confronting strong, gusty crosswinds during takeoff.
- Limitations in simulator training, which did not realistically prepare crews for the amount and timing of rudder control needed in such conditions.

Investigators also examined whether the crew should have delayed the takeoff or selected another runway. The board found that the pilots had not been given information showing that the actual crosswind had risen to the level later reconstructed.

### No single mechanical failure found

The aircraft’s engines, flight controls, nose-wheel steering and braking systems were examined. Investigators did not find a pre-existing mechanical malfunction that caused the airplane to leave the runway.

The breakup and fire were attributed to impacts after the runway excursion. The aircraft was destroyed and written off.

### Safety changes follow

The accident prompted scrutiny of how airports report rapidly changing wind conditions and how airlines train pilots for crosswind takeoffs. Recommendations called for better dissemination of runway-specific wind information, improved simulator scenarios and clearer procedures for maintaining directional control during severe gusts.

The investigation ultimately portrayed the crash as a combination of a sudden environmental threat and an insufficient cockpit response—not a structural failure of the Boeing 737.

Despite the violent runway departure, extensive damage and post-crash fire, every person aboard survived, making the evacuation one of the central lessons of the accident.
